::: {.research-theme}
## Temporal dynamics of heat damage and recovery

Most studies of photosynthetic heat tolerance treat the crossing of thermal safety margins as causing instantaneous and irreversible damage, but real heat damage and recovery unfolds over time. Using a custom-built leaf heater (affectionately referred to as the panini press) to expose leaves to acute, controlled heat stress in-situ, combined with repeated measurements of light- and dark-adapted fluorescence, I am exploring variation in these temporal dynamics and using observed trends to inform the incorporation of this process into the individual-based forest model TROLL.
:::

::: {.research-theme}
## Leaf phenology, age, and thermal sensitivity

Most studies of plant responses to heat and drought (and generally all functional traits) focus on mature leaves, yet scaling physiological responses to whole-plant performance and ecosystem carbon cycling requires accounting for leaf ontogeny and demography. At AMAP I joined the [PhenObs](https://umr-ecofog.cirad.fr/projets/phenobs) and [CoForFunc](https://coforfunc.eu/) projects to examine how leaf age–trait relationships shape leaf longevity and optimal flushing strategies. The [CanObs network](https://canobs.net/about) uses repeat drone-based imaging of individual tree canopies to monitor phenophases, and — combined with expert assessment of branch growth markers — allows the age of individual leaves to be determined. Using a dataset of leaf traits (photosynthetic capacity, turgor loss point, and leaf morphology) measured across a range of leaf ages, I simulated how this observed variation affects the optimal timing of leaf flushing, and assessed how well these simulations matched observed patterns.

During this work it became apparent that climate variation and leaf age are often confounded in seasonal observational trait datasets, making it difficult to isolate the "real" age trajectory of traits like photosynthetic capacity. In addition, we know very little about how the temperature sensitivity of photosynthesis itself varies across leaf age, making attempts to account for climate acclimation potentially biased. During my current fellowship I am extending this work to investigate how leaf age influences leaf energy balance and seasonal acclimation of photosynthetic temperature optima in African tropical tree species, aiming to separate age-dependent physiological variation from climate acclimation responses.

**In preparation:** Middleby, Barbier, Heuret & Maréchaux
:::

::: {.research-theme}
## Decoupling of photosynthesis and stomatal conductance at high temperatures

Currently, climate–vegetation models used to simulate carbon and water fluxes in forests assume photosynthesis and stomatal conductance are tightly coupled. However, a growing number of studies have documented a maintenance or even increase in stomatal conductance at high temperatures, even as photosynthesis declines. While stomatal opening can cool leaves under extreme heat, it also increases hydraulic risk — raising the question of whether heat avoidance and drought tolerance are coordinated strategies in tropical trees. As an Ernst Mayr Fellow at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, I used elevational gradients in Panama to test photosynthetic and stomatal responses to leaf temperatures up to 50°C, providing in-situ evidence of stomatal re-opening at extreme leaf temperatures. At the same time, I've been testing whether the same pattern holds at the ecosystem level, using generalised additive models with eddy covariance data from flux towers. I've presented this work at the New Phytologist Next Generation Scientists symposium (Birmingham), EGU (Vienna), and the New Phytologist Extreme Heat symposium (Córdoba).

**In review:** Middleby, Rojas-González & Slot &nbsp;·&nbsp; **In preparation:** Middleby, Rifai & Cernusak
:::

::: {.research-theme}
## Patterns and drivers of thermoregulation

A key question is whether trees can actively regulate leaf temperature to avoid heat stress. During my PhD, I investigated the role of intraspecific trait variation in mediating leaf thermoregulation in tropical rainforest trees, combining experimental (climate-controlled glasshouse) and field-based approaches (elevation gradients, common garden trials). Using leaf-to-air temperature differences (ΔT) as a quantitative phenotype, I combined this with genome-wide association analysis and generalised dissimilarity modelling to show that divergent selection linked to both temperature and moisture underlies patterns of thermoregulatory trait variation — evidence of local adaptation operating on this trait. In a complementary [common garden trial](https://tropadapt.org/) using provenances sourced from cool and warm source populations, I found ecotypic variation in heat tolerance and leaf–air temperature differences driven by leaf energy balance traits — but this didn't translate into differences in thermal safety margins when measured side by side. A third study then used a climate-controlled glasshouse to test whether temperature or VPD better explained the acclimation responses observed across the elevation gradient. This work was featured on the cover of *Global Change Biology*, in a companion piece in *The Conversation*, and in an article in the Rainforest Rescue newsletter.

**Key publications:** Middleby et al. 2025, *Global Change Biology* ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.70461)) · Middleby et al. 2025, *Plant, Cell & Environment* ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/pce.15141)) · Middleby et al. 2024, *New Phytologist* ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.19822))
:::

::: {.research-theme}
## Effect of in-situ leaf warming on carbon uptake in tropical trees

Lowland tropical forests are projected to experience sustained warming over coming decades, raising the question of whether mature canopy trees can acclimate sufficiently to maintain carbon uptake. With Kristine Crous, I helped run one of the longest-running in-situ leaf-warming experiments in a tropical rainforest, continuously heating upper-canopy leaves by +4°C in the Daintree Rainforest, Australia. Both stomatal conductance and photosynthesis were strongly reduced under warming, with no shift in the thermal optimum of photosynthesis, while respiration rates (R25 and Q10) did not change in response to warming. Together, this combination of physiological responses to leaf warming in mature tropical trees may point to a reduced carbon sink under future warming in tropical forests. This work was featured in [a Conversation article I wrote with Kristine Crous](https://shorturl.at/iGujv). I was also a co-author on a related study led by Chris Doughty, which modelled how the distribution of leaf temperatures across the tropics shifts under warming — identifying a potential tipping point for the Amazon rainforest. Considered alongside the physiological findings above, it points to a shared concern for the future carbon sink capacity of tropical forests as they warm.

**Key publications:** Doughty et al. 2023, *Nature* ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06391-z)) · Crous et al. 2023, *Tree Physiology* ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/treephys/tpad054)) · Crous, Middleby et al. 2025, *New Phytologist* ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.20320))
:::

::: {.research-theme}
## Bachelor's thesis: oxygen isotopes as a proxy for leaf temperature

This is where the thermoregulation question started for me. During my B.Sc. at the University of Göttingen I tested whether oxygen isotopes in leaf cellulose could serve as a proxy for photosynthesis-weighted canopy leaf temperature — combining field measurements of leaf temperature and gas exchange across a temperate forest's vertical canopy gradient with stable oxygen isotope sampling and eddy covariance data. The work showed that cellulose isotope signals were confounded by carryover from the previous year's source water early in the growing season, limiting their use as a clean seasonal temperature proxy.

*Presented at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting, New Orleans, 2021 (nominated for a student presentation award).*
:::
